wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c0.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: Polar ice comes in different kinds. Ice sheets are vast domes of compacted snow on land, kilometres thick; today only Greenland and Antarctica have them.\n\nSea ice is frozen seawater, usually only a few metres thick. Ice shelves are the floating edges of ice sheets, and icebergs break off from them.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c1.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: Sea ice grows and shrinks with the seasons. Arctic ice peaks in March and is smallest in September; Antarctic ice does the opposite.\n\nEach winter the sea around Antarctica freezes over an area larger than the continent itself, then most of it melts again. This yearly pulse is one of the biggest seasonal changes on Earth.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c2.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, and three of the claims overlap. Most other countries, including Portugal, do not recognise any claim.\n\nThe Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959, puts these claims on hold. Antarctica is the only continent where no country exercises full sovereignty.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c3.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: Unlike Antarctica, the Arctic has no special treaty. Its lands belong to eight countries, and its ocean is governed by the international law of the sea.\n\nEach coastal state controls fishing and resources up to 200 nautical miles out. Several are asking to extend their seabed rights all the way to the North Pole.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c4.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: About four million people live in the Arctic, in towns, mining cities and small villages. Around one in ten belongs to an Indigenous people, such as the Inuit, Sámi, Nenets or Chukchi.\n\nMany Arctic communities now govern themselves, combining modern life with hunting, herding and their own languages.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c5.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: The two polar regions take turns. When the Arctic has its midnight sun in June, Antarctica is deep in polar night, and six months later they swap.\n\nLong twilights soften the change, and in the dark months auroras often light up the sky near both poles.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c6.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: About 30 countries run around 70 research stations in Antarctica. In summer several thousand people live there; in winter about a thousand stay.\n\nIn the Arctic, scientists work in towns and remote camps, from the international village of Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard to stations in Greenland, Canada and Alaska.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c7.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: Snow falling on ice sheets traps tiny bubbles of air. Layer by layer it builds an archive of the atmosphere going back hundreds of thousands of years.\n\nBy drilling cores kilometres long, scientists can read past temperatures and greenhouse gas levels, and show how unusual today's levels are.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c8.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: As Arctic sea ice shrinks, routes along the top of Russia and through Canada's islands stay open longer each summer. They can cut the sea journey between Europe and East Asia by about a third.\n\nTraffic is still small, because ice, darkness, storms and a lack of ports make them risky and costly.

wo-poles.title: wo-poles.c9.text
The Arctic and Antarctica: Sea level is rising for two main reasons: warmer water takes up more space, and ice on land is melting into the ocean. Greenland and Antarctica are losing hundreds of billions of tonnes of ice a year.\n\nThe rise is speeding up, threatening low coasts, including stretches of Portugal's.
